Text: QuadConnect is a social app for students at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. It helps you meet people in person instead of scrolling through profiles. Each week the app gives you one planned meetup on a weekend, either with one other student or with a squad of four to eight students. The meetup happens at an approved place on campus, at a time that everyone in it marked as free, and it comes with a suggested activity to get things started. QuadConnect builds these matches from the interests you share with other students and from the weekend hours you are free.

The idea is fewer, better meetings with people who like what you like, rather than an endless feed of strangers. QuadConnect is a closed community for verified Illinois students. Every student profile is tied to one university NetID and one illinois.edu email address, and the app allows only one profile per NetID, so the same person cannot join twice. A NetID and its email address must belong together, and the app refuses a profile that pairs a NetID with someone else's mailbox. A profile also carries a verified flag. Only verified students take part in the weekly matching, and a student whose verification is removed leaves the matching pool.

The current prototype signs you in with a username and password or with Google, and it was built so that the university's own single sign-on can replace that later without changing your profile. QuadConnect is a student project. Team 13, The Connectors, built it for INFO 490 at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and this handbook describes its first prototype. In the prototype, the student profiles, matches and feedback you see are sample data, loaded so that every page has something to show. The rules described here are the ones the app follows today: which details a profile holds, which times you can choose, where meetups can happen, how venue suggestions are checked and what happens to your feedback.
Where a part of the app uses artificial intelligence, the handbook says so and explains what the AI does and what it never decides.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Text: You can create a QuadConnect account in two ways. The first is to sign up with a username, an email address and a password. QuadConnect stores your password only as a salted hash, so nobody who runs the site can read it. The second is to choose Continue with Google on the login page and use your Google account instead. To log in later, you can type either your username or your email address with your password, and you can tick Remember me to stay signed in. Almost every page of QuadConnect needs you to be logged in.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Text: The only pages open to everyone are the landing page, the privacy notice, the login and sign-up pages, and one public summary of interests. When you continue with Google, Google sends QuadConnect four things: your name, your email address, a link to your profile picture and your Google account number. QuadConnect asks Google for nothing else. It does not see your contacts, your files or your calendar, and it never sees your Google password, because you type that into Google's own page. If you later want QuadConnect to stop using your Google account, remove QuadConnect from the third-party connections in your Google account settings.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Text: Your QuadConnect profile is kept separate from the way you sign in, which is why the app can offer both Google and a password today and move to university sign-in later. QuadConnect cannot send email yet, so it cannot send you a password reset link. If you forget your password and you signed up with Google, simply use Continue with Google on the login page. Otherwise, email the address given on the Privacy page, and the team will set a new password for you. QuadConnect uses only two cookies. One keeps you logged in between pages, and the other protects forms, so that another website cannot submit a form on QuadConnect in your name.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Text: There are no tracking cookies, no analytics cookies and no advertising cookies. When you finish, use the Log out button next to your username at the top of the page.

Your profile starts with where you study. You give your college, such as the Grainger College of Engineering or the Gies College of Business, and you can add your major or program, such as Computer Science. The colleges in the prototype are the Grainger College of Engineering, the Gies College of Business, the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, the College of Media, the College of Applied Health Sciences and the College of Fine and Applied Arts. You can also add an on-campus or near-campus part-time job. A job is optional and counts only as a soft signal in matching, never as a requirement.

Next you pick your interests from one shared list, so that a word like Gaming means the same thing for every student and shared interests can be counted. The list has three kinds of entries. Hobbies are Art, Basketball, Fitness, Food, Gaming, Movies, Music, Outdoors, Photography, Reading, Technology and Travel. Registered student organizations, or RSOs, are Business Illini, Engineers Without Borders, Habitat for Humanity UIUC, Illini Media, Illini Robotics, Illinois Student Government, the Indian Students Association, UIUC Dance Marathon, UIUC Esports and the UIUC Pre-Med Society. Meeting activities are Board games, Campus walk, Coffee, Food, Sports and Study or social space. You cannot pick the same entry twice.

Not every interest matters equally to you, so QuadConnect lets you star the few you care about most. A starred interest is weighted more heavily when the app looks for your match, so two students who both starred Basketball count as a stronger fit than two students who merely ticked it. Your other picks still count, just less. The QuadConnect team can also retire an interest when the option is no longer offered. A retired interest disappears from the list for new picks, but students who already chose it keep it in their history, so past matches can still explain why they happened. An entry that students have already selected cannot be deleted outright, only retired.

Then you choose how you want to meet. Friend Connect is a one-on-one meetup with a single other student, for people who prefer a quieter, more personal conversation. Squad Connect is a meetup with a small group of four to eight students, for people who like a livelier table and less pressure on any one conversation. If you do not choose, your profile starts on Friend Connect. Your choice tells the matching which kind of experience to build for you each week, and the match you receive carries the same connection type. You can think of Friend Connect as a coffee with one new friend, and Squad Connect as a small group outing.

The social preferences tell QuadConnect what kind of company suits you. Social energy is a five-step scale: Quiet or low-key, Somewhat quiet, Balanced, Fairly social and Very social. A new profile starts at Balanced, in the middle of the scale. Conversation style is Casual conversations, Deep conversations or Activity-focused, where the activity matters more than the talk, and casual is the default. Group size is One person, Small group of three to five, or Either, with Either as the default. Three yes-or-no questions finish the page. The first asks whether you are comfortable being matched with students within one year of your age, and it starts as yes.

The second asks whether shared RSO membership should count more heavily, and it starts as no. The third asks whether you are open to meeting students from other colleges, and it starts as yes. You can change any of these answers whenever your preferences change.

QuadConnect meetups happen only on weekends, so your availability is a set of weekend time windows. You can mark Saturday, Sunday or both, and each day has four two-hour windows: 10 AM to 12 PM, 12 to 2 PM, 2 to 4 PM and 4 to 6 PM. That gives eight possible slots in a week, and you can mark as many of them as you like. Each slot can be marked only once, so marking Saturday from 2 to 4 PM twice is not possible. All the windows fall in the daytime, between 10 AM and 6 PM, so every QuadConnect meetup takes place during the day. Availability is the one hard rule in matching.

Two students can be matched only if they share at least one free slot, because a meetup needs a time that everyone can make. Interests and preferences decide how good a match is, but a shared slot decides whether a match is possible at all. That makes your availability the most important part of your profile to keep up to date. If you mark only one slot, the app can only match you with students who are free at that exact time. Marking more windows, or both weekend days, gives the matching many more people to choose from and makes a match each week more likely.

QuadConnect works in weekly cycles. A matching week starts on a Monday, and each cycle produces a small number of scheduled meetings rather than a feed you browse. Each match is one real meeting: one approved place, one date and time, and the students taking part. It also has a connection type, Friend Connect or Squad Connect, and it may come with a suggested activity, such as a campus walk or board games, to break the ice. You receive one match per week. On the Matches page you can see your match with its place, time, participants, check-in code and status.

For every student in a match, QuadConnect records a fit score from 0 to 100 that says how well that student fits the rest of the group. The score reflects what the students have in common: shared interests, with starred interests counting more, shared free times and compatible social preferences. Next to the score, the match keeps a short, readable reason, such as Basketball, Gaming and Coffee. The match page shows it under Matched on, so you can see why you were put together. A high score means a strong overlap with the others, not a promise that you will become friends, and the reasons are often the easiest way to start the first conversation.

A match moves through four stages. It starts as Proposed, when it has been offered to the students in it. Each student then answers. Your answer starts as Awaiting response, and you either accept, which confirms your attendance, or decline. When the students have accepted, the match becomes Confirmed. After the meetup has happened it becomes Completed, and a match that will not take place is marked Cancelled. If you cannot make it, decline rather than simply not turning up. Declining is how you are withdrawn from a meetup that other students are still planning to attend, and a student cannot be dropped from a match in progress without that explicit step.

This matters most in a squad, where several people plan their weekend around the group. A clear decline lets the others know who is coming, while a silent no-show leaves them waiting at the venue and wondering whether the meetup is still on. Squad matches bring four to eight students together, so they need more planning than a one-on-one coffee. Every venue records the largest group it can seat comfortably, from 2 to 50 people, so that a squad is planned for a place that fits it. A squad is also a good setting for the suggested activity, because a shared task such as board games or sports takes the pressure off the conversation.
Your group size preference matters here as well. A student who chose One person as their group size suits Friend Connect, while a student who chose Small group suits a squad.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Text: Every QuadConnect meetup takes place at an approved campus location. Safety is a design principle of the app: meetings happen only at vetted, public, staffed places, and the list of places is kept by the QuadConnect team rather than typed in by students. The approved venues in the prototype are the Illini Union at 1401 W Green St in Urbana, the Grainger Engineering Library at 1301 W Springfield Ave in Urbana, the Main Quad at 601 S Wright St in Champaign, and Espresso Royale on Goodwin at 1117 W Oregon St in Urbana. On the Campus locations page you can filter the list to indoor or outdoor venues, or to venues that seat at least a given number of people.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Text: Each venue page tells you how to find your group. It gives the street address, says whether the place is indoors or outdoors and how many people it seats, and adds an arrival note that says exactly where to wait. At the Illini Union you meet at the main entrance, in the ground floor lobby. At the Grainger Engineering Library you meet in the first floor commons. At the Main Quad, the only outdoor venue, you meet at the south end, by the Alma Mater statue. At Espresso Royale on Goodwin you meet in the counter seating area. The Illini Union seats twelve people, the Grainger Engineering Library eight, the Main Quad twenty and Espresso Royale six.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Text: A full squad of eight therefore fits every venue except Espresso Royale, which suits Friend Connect meetups and smaller squads. If you are not sure where to go, open the venue page from your match before you leave, because the arrival note is written for exactly that moment. When you arrive, you check in with your match's check-in code. Every match has its own short code, in a form such as QC-4827, which appears on the match page. Entering the code records the time you checked in. Check-in matters for two reasons. It lets your group see who has arrived, since the match page lists every participant with their check-in time.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Text: It also confirms that the meetup really took place, which is part of the record of the match along with its status and the feedback that follows. If the others have not checked in yet, wait at the spot named in the arrival note. Every match has an Icebreakers page with trivia questions to get the conversation going. QuadConnect picks the questions from what your group has in common. It looks at the interests the members chose, finds one that matches a trivia topic, and fetches questions on that topic from the Open Trivia Database. The page says which shared interest it picked and how many members chose it.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Text: If no shared interest matches a trivia topic, you get general knowledge questions instead. Each answer stays hidden until you choose to show it, and reloading the page brings new questions. If the questions cannot be loaded, reload the page in a few seconds to try again.

If you know a public place that would suit a meetup, you can suggest it on the Campus locations page. The form asks for the venue's name, its street address, an optional note on where to meet, whether it is indoors, and how many seats it has, from 2 to 50. Name a public, staffed place on or near campus. Every suggestion is saved as not approved and waits for review by the QuadConnect staff. Until a staff member approves it, the suggestion is visible to staff only, and no meetup can be scheduled there. A suggestion can never approve itself, because the form has no approval field, and staff approve venues in the admin site.

The form checks your suggestion before it is saved. A venue that is already listed, or already waiting for review, is refused, and the form asks you to check the list or name a different place. A missing name or street address is refused with a message that shows an example, such as Illini Union at 1401 W Green St, Urbana. The number of seats must be a whole number from 2 to 50, because a meetup needs at least two seats. If any field is wrong, nothing is saved, the field is marked, and you can fix it and send the suggestion again. When you send a suggestion, QuadConnect also runs an automatic check.

The venue's name, address and meeting note go to an outside AI service, Groq, which advises whether the place looks suitable, needs a closer look, or is likely unsuitable, with a one-line reason. The check can also raise flags: private residence, isolated or unsafe, alcohol or nightlife, far from campus, unclear details, advertising or spam, contact details, and manipulation attempt. The check only advises. It never approves a venue, and staff see its advice next to the suggestion when they decide. The automatic check is built to err on the side of caution, and its advice can only become stricter, never looser.

A serious flag, such as private residence, isolated or unsafe, alcohol or nightlife, or advertising or spam, means the advice can be no better than needs a closer look, even if the AI called the place suitable. Contact details in a suggestion have the same effect. A suggestion that tries to give the AI instructions is treated as a manipulation attempt and is marked likely unsuitable. Before anything is sent to the AI service, email addresses, phone numbers and links are removed from the text, and the student who made the suggestion is never named. The staff member reviewing the suggestion sees the advice, the flags and the reason, and then decides.
That keeps a person responsible for every venue students are sent to, while the automatic check catches the obvious problems early.

The Search students page lets you filter the roster of verified students by name, interest, college, connection type or venue. Your search is kept in the page address, so you can bookmark it or share the link. If you need one particular student, use the NetID lookup instead. The NetID you type stays out of the page address, so it is not saved in your browser history. When a filter has a value that is not in its list, the page asks you to pick a value from the list. If nothing matches, it suggests trying fewer filters or a shorter search term. Below the results, the search page summarizes the students it found.

It shows how many students matched out of all verified students, their average social energy on the scale from 1, quiet, to 5, very social, and how many colleges they come from, with a table of students per college. It also lists the interests most shared among the students in the results, with the category and the number of students for each. This summary is a quick way to see what a group of students has in common. A search for one college, for example, shows which interests are most popular there. If you would rather describe the students you want in your own words, use Ask in plain English.

You type a request such as students who like basketball and are free on Saturday morning, and a language model turns it into search filters. The page shows exactly which filters the model chose, so you can check how it read your request, and students with more of the requested interests come first. The model runs on QuadConnect's own server, so your request is not sent to any outside service. The first search after the server starts takes longer while the model loads. Ask in plain English has two safeguards.

If the language model is switched off on the server, a simple keyword parser reads your request instead, and the page tells you so, because a keyword parser may miss part of what you asked for. If your request contains instructions aimed at the AI, such as telling it to ignore its rules, those instructions are ignored, because the model can only choose from the search filters the page offers. If no filter can be found in your request, the page asks you to name an interest or a club, a college, a day or time on the weekend, or how social the students are.

After a meetup you can leave private feedback about the experience. You give an overall rating from one to five stars and tick what you enjoyed: the conversation, the shared interests and the activity, and whether you felt comfortable. You can also write a private note. The note is never shown to the other students in your match, and neither is your rating. Each student leaves at most one review for each experience, because feedback belongs to your place in that one meetup. QuadConnect uses feedback to improve the quality of future matches, so honest answers help the app learn what works for you. Feedback is also how a one-off meetup can turn into a lasting connection.

In your feedback you can say that you want to stay connected with the people you met. This works as a mutual opt-in, which means a connection forms only if both sides say yes. If you say yes and the other student does not, nothing happens and nobody is told, so there is no awkward rejection. Because your choice stays private unless it is mutual, you can answer honestly, whether the meetup was the start of a friendship or simply a pleasant afternoon. The Feedback summary page shows what students think of QuadConnect as a whole, without revealing anyone's answers.

It reports the number of feedback submissions, the average rating out of five, the share of students who want to stay connected, the spread of ratings from one to five stars, and what students enjoyed. Individual ratings and private notes are never displayed. Before any feedback exists, the page says that feedback will appear once students complete a match and submit their post-experience feedback. The landing page also shows the average experience rating.

QuadConnect is designed around safety. Every meetup is at an approved, public venue, never at someone's home, and every meetup is on a weekend during the day, between 10 AM and 6 PM. Only verified Illinois students take part in matching, so everyone you meet is a fellow student. Venue suggestions are reviewed by staff, and the automatic check flags places that look private, isolated, unsafe or tied to alcohol and nightlife. Stay at the approved venue named on your match page rather than moving the meetup somewhere else. Use your check-in code when you arrive, so the match records who came. A good meetup depends on everyone showing up.

Accept your match only if you can make it, and decline as early as you can if your plans change, since other students may be planning around you, especially in a squad. Arrive on time and read the arrival note on the venue page, so the group does not have to search for you. Be respectful of different backgrounds, colleges and social styles, because QuadConnect deliberately brings together students who might not have met otherwise. Afterwards, leave honest feedback, including whether you felt comfortable, because that answer helps QuadConnect improve future matches.

QuadConnect keeps only what it needs. For your account it keeps your username, your email address and your password, stored as a salted hash. If you continue with Google, it keeps the name, email address, profile picture link and Google account number that Google sends. Your student profile holds your NetID, your illinois.edu address, your college and department, your interests, your preferences and your free times. Matching uses the interests and free times on student profiles, and in this first prototype those profiles are sample data. QuadConnect sets only two cookies, one to keep you logged in and one to protect its forms. Nothing about you is sold or shared.

QuadConnect's one public API, the interest summary at /api/summary/, publishes only how many students picked each interest, never names, NetIDs or email addresses. The site is hosted on PythonAnywhere, and Google handles Continue with Google. Two features use AI. Ask in plain English runs a language model on QuadConnect's own server, so your searches are not sent anywhere. Venue suggestions are checked by an outside AI service, Groq, but only after email addresses, phone numbers and links are removed, and without the name of the student who sent the suggestion. You stay in control of your data. To delete your account and everything stored with it, email the address given on the Privacy page.

To stop QuadConnect from using your Google account, remove it from the third-party connections in your Google account settings. The student lists that staff can download for reports leave out email addresses. The Privacy page explains all of this in full, and it was last updated on 19 October 2026. If a feature changes what QuadConnect keeps or shares, the Privacy page is where that change is described.

QuadConnect has a few pages that describe the community as a whole. The Insights page draws charts of who is on QuadConnect and what they are into, such as students per college and interest categories, and every chart comes with a text description and a table of the same numbers. The Reports page counts students per college, split by preferred connection type, and matches per venue, split into completed and upcoming meetups. It also lets you download the student list as a CSV or JSON file, sorted by name, with each student's matching preferences, interests and number of matches. Email addresses are never included in these downloads. For developers, QuadConnect offers a small API, described on its API page.

It lists the approved venues, as JSON and as plain text, and the matches. It also publishes summary numbers, such as how many students picked each interest and how many matches were made each week, and it serves icebreaker questions for a match. Only the interest summary is public. Every other part of the API needs you to be logged in, like the rest of the site. The public summary can be open to anyone because it never contains names, NetIDs or email addresses, only counts.

Can I choose who I meet? Not directly. QuadConnect gives you one planned match each week instead of a list of people to pick from, because the aim is a real meeting rather than endless browsing. What you control are the signals your match is built from: your interests and the ones you star, your connection type, your social preferences and, above all, your free weekend slots. You can also search the roster of verified students to see who is on QuadConnect. If you want to meet students with a particular interest, star that interest and make sure your free times overlap with theirs. What happens if my free times do not overlap with anyone?

Then QuadConnect cannot match you that week, because a shared free slot is the one hard rule of matching. Nothing else can make up for it, and two students with every interest in common still cannot be matched without a slot in common. The fix is to mark more of the eight weekend windows, which run from 10 AM to 6 PM on Saturday and Sunday. Students who mark both days and several windows give the matching the most room. Your interests and preferences then decide which of the possible matches fits you best. Can we meet at a place that is not on the list? No.

Every QuadConnect meetup is scheduled at an approved campus location, and the match page names the place. If you know a good public place that is not on the list, suggest it on the Campus locations page. Staff review every suggestion, helped by an automatic check that looks for problems such as private homes or nightlife venues, and only approved venues are used for matches. Until a suggestion is approved it stays visible to staff only. Moving a meetup to an unapproved place on your own means stepping outside the protections QuadConnect is built on. Does an AI decide anything about me? QuadConnect uses AI in two places, and neither makes decisions about you.

Ask in plain English uses a language model on QuadConnect's own server to turn a search request into filters, and it shows you the filters it chose. The venue check uses an outside AI service to advise staff about a suggested meeting place, but staff make the decision, and the check never approves a venue by itself. Your matches are built from your profile, your interests and your free times, and your feedback stays private. Who can see my feedback and my notes? Nobody else in your match can see your rating, your ticks or your private note, and your choice about staying connected stays private unless the other student makes the same choice.

The Feedback summary page shows only totals and averages across all students, such as the average rating and the share who want to stay connected. Individual ratings and private notes are never displayed anywhere in the app. QuadConnect uses feedback to improve future matches, so the most useful feedback is honest, including whether you felt comfortable during the meetup.

A retired interest disappears from the list for new picks, but students who already chose it keep it in their history, so past matches can still explain why they happened. An entry that students have already selected cannot be deleted outright, only retired.

Then you choose how you want to meet. Friend Connect is a one-on-one meetup with a single other student, for people who prefer a quieter, more personal conversation. Squad Connect is a meetup with a small group of four to eight students, for people who like a livelier table and less pressure on any one conversation. The social preferences tell QuadConnect what kind of company suits you. Social energy is a five-step scale: Quiet or low-key, Somewhat quiet, Balanced, Fairly social and Very social. A new profile starts at Balanced, in the middle of the scale. Conversation style is Casual conversations, Deep conversations or Activity-focused, where the activity matters more than the talk, and casual is the default. Group size is One person, Small group of three to five, or Either, with Either as the default. Three yes-or-no questions finish the page. The first asks whether you are comfortable being matched with students within one year of your age, and it starts as yes. The second asks whether shared RSO membership should count more heavily, and it starts as no. The third asks whether you are open to meeting students from other colleges, and it starts as yes. You can change any of these answers whenever your preferences change.

QuadConnect meetups happen only on weekends, so your availability is a set of weekend time windows. You can mark Saturday, Sunday or both, and each day has four two-hour windows: 10 AM to 12 PM, 12 to 2 PM, 2 to 4 PM and 4 to 6 PM. That gives eight possible slots in a week, and you can mark as many of them as you like. Each slot can be marked only once, so marking Saturday from 2 to 4 PM twice is not possible. All the windows fall in the daytime, between 10 AM and 6 PM, so every QuadConnect meetup takes place during the day.

Availability is the one hard rule in matching. Two students can be matched only if they share at least one free slot, because a meetup needs a time that everyone can make. Interests and preferences decide how good a match is, but a shared slot decides whether a match is possible at all. That makes your availability the most important part of your profile to keep up to date. If you mark only one slot, the app can only match you with students who are free at that exact time. Marking more windows, or both weekend days, gives the matching many more people to choose from and makes a match each week more likely.

QuadConnect works in weekly cycles. A matching week starts on a Monday, and each cycle produces a small number of scheduled meetings rather than a feed you browse. Each match is one real meeting: one approved place, one date and time, and the students taking part. It also has a connection type, Friend Connect or Squad Connect, and it may come with a suggested activity, such as a campus walk or board games, to break the ice. You receive one match per week. On the Matches page you can see your match with its place, time, participants, check-in code and status.

For every student in a match, QuadConnect records a fit score from 0 to 100 that says how well that student fits the rest of the group. The score reflects what the students have in common: shared interests, with starred interests counting more, shared free times and compatible social preferences. Next to the score, the match keeps a short, readable reason, such as Basketball, Gaming and Coffee. The match page shows it under Matched on, so you can see why you were put together. A high score means a strong overlap with the others, not a promise that you will become friends, and the reasons are often the easiest way to start the first conversation.

A match moves through four stages. It starts as Proposed, when it has been offered to the students in it. Each student then answers. Your answer starts as Awaiting response, and you either accept, which confirms your attendance, or decline. When the students have accepted, the match becomes Confirmed. After the meetup has happened it becomes Completed, and a match that will not take place is marked Cancelled. If you cannot make it, decline rather than simply not turning up. Declining is how you are withdrawn from a meetup that other students are still planning to attend, and a student cannot be dropped from a match in progress without that explicit step. This matters most in a squad, where several people plan their weekend around the group. A clear decline lets the others know who is coming, while a silent no-show leaves them waiting at the venue and wondering whether the meetup is still on.

Squad matches bring four to eight students together, so they need more planning than a one-on-one coffee. Every venue records the largest group it can seat comfortably, from 2 to 50 people, so that a squad is planned for a place that fits it. A squad is also a good setting for the suggested activity, because a shared task such as board games or sports takes the pressure off the conversation. Your group size preference matters here as well. A student who chose One person as their group size suits Friend Connect, while a student who chose Small group suits a squad.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Text:
Every QuadConnect meetup takes place at an approved campus location. Safety is a design principle of the app: meetings happen only at vetted, public, staffed places, and the list of places is kept by the QuadConnect team rather than typed in by students. The approved venues in the prototype are the Illini Union at 1401 W Green St in Urbana, the Grainger Engineering Library at 1301 W Springfield Ave in Urbana, the Main Quad at 601 S Wright St in Champaign, and Espresso Royale on Goodwin at 1117 W Oregon St in Urbana. On the Campus locations page you can filter the list to indoor or outdoor venues, or to venues that seat at least a given number of people.

Each venue page tells you how to find your group. It gives the street address, says whether the place is indoors or outdoors and how many people it seats, and adds an arrival note that says exactly where to wait. At the Illini Union you meet at the main entrance, in the ground floor lobby. At the Grainger Engineering Library you meet in the first floor commons. At the Main Quad, the only outdoor venue, you meet at the south end, by the Alma Mater statue. At Espresso Royale on Goodwin you meet in the counter seating area. The Illini Union seats twelve people, the Grainger Engineering Library eight, the Main Quad twenty and Espresso Royale six. A full squad of eight therefore fits every venue except Espresso Royale, which suits Friend Connect meetups and smaller squads. If you are not sure where to go, open the venue page from your match before you leave, because the arrival note is written for exactly that moment.

Every match has an Icebreakers page with trivia questions to get the conversation going. QuadConnect picks the questions from what your group has in common. It looks at the interests the members chose, finds one that matches a trivia topic, and fetches questions on that topic from the Open Trivia Database. The page says which shared interest it picked and how many members chose it. If no shared interest matches a trivia topic, you get general knowledge questions instead. Each answer stays hidden until you choose to show it, and reloading the page brings new questions. If the questions cannot be loaded, reload the page in a few seconds to try again.

If you know a public place that would suit a meetup, you can suggest it on the Campus locations page. The form asks for the venue's name, its street address, an optional note on where to meet, whether it is indoors, and how many seats it has, from 2 to 50. Name a public, staffed place on or near campus. Every suggestion is saved as not approved and waits for review by the QuadConnect staff. Until a staff member approves it, the suggestion is visible to staff only, and no meetup can be scheduled there. A suggestion can never approve itself, because the form has no approval field, and staff approve venues in the admin site.

The form checks your suggestion before it is saved. A venue that is already listed, or already waiting for review, is refused, and the form asks you to check the list or name a different place. A missing name or street address is refused with a message that shows an example, such as Illini Union at 1401 W Green St, Urbana. The number of seats must be a whole number from 2 to 50, because a meetup needs at least two seats. If any field is wrong, nothing is saved, the field is marked, and you can fix it and send the suggestion again.

When you send a suggestion, QuadConnect also runs an automatic check. The venue's name, address and meeting note go to an outside AI service, Groq, which advises whether the place looks suitable, needs a closer look, or is likely unsuitable, with a one-line reason. The check can also raise flags: private residence, isolated or unsafe, alcohol or nightlife, far from campus, unclear details, advertising or spam, contact details, and manipulation attempt. The check only advises. It never approves a venue, and staff see its advice next to the suggestion when they decide.

The automatic check is built to err on the side of caution, and its advice can only become stricter, never looser. A serious flag, such as private residence, isolated or unsafe, alcohol or nightlife, or advertising or spam, means the advice can be no better than needs a closer look, even if the AI called the place suitable. Contact details in a suggestion have the same effect. A suggestion that tries to give the AI instructions is treated as a manipulation attempt and is marked likely unsuitable. Before anything is sent to the AI service, email addresses, phone numbers and links are removed from the text, and the student who made the suggestion is never named. The staff member reviewing the suggestion sees the advice, the flags and the reason, and then decides. That keeps a person responsible for every venue students are sent to, while the automatic check catches the obvious problems early.

The Search students page lets you filter the roster of verified students by name, interest, college, connection type or venue. Your search is kept in the page address, so you can bookmark it or share the link. If you need one particular student, use the NetID lookup instead. The NetID you type stays out of the page address, so it is not saved in your browser history. When a filter has a value that is not in its list, the page asks you to pick a value from the list. If nothing matches, it suggests trying fewer filters or a shorter search term.

Below the results, the search page summarizes the students it found. It shows how many students matched out of all verified students, their average social energy on the scale from 1, quiet, to 5, very social, and how many colleges they come from, with a table of students per college. It also lists the interests most shared among the students in the results, with the category and the number of students for each. This summary is a quick way to see what a group of students has in common. A search for one college, for example, shows which interests are most popular there.

Ask in plain English has two safeguards. If the language model is switched off on the server, a simple keyword parser reads your request instead, and the page tells you so, because a keyword parser may miss part of what you asked for. If your request contains instructions aimed at the AI, such as telling it to ignore its rules, those instructions are ignored, because the model can only choose from the search filters the page offers. If no filter can be found in your request, the page asks you to name an interest or a club, a college, a day or time on the weekend, or how social the students are.

After a meetup you can leave private feedback about the experience. You give an overall rating from one to five stars and tick what you enjoyed: the conversation, the shared interests and the activity, and whether you felt comfortable. You can also write a private note. The note is never shown to the other students in your match, and neither is your rating. Each student leaves at most one review for each experience, because feedback belongs to your place in that one meetup. QuadConnect uses feedback to improve the quality of future matches, so honest answers help the app learn what works for you.

Feedback is also how a one-off meetup can turn into a lasting connection. In your feedback you can say that you want to stay connected with the people you met. This works as a mutual opt-in, which means a connection forms only if both sides say yes. If you say yes and the other student does not, nothing happens and nobody is told, so there is no awkward rejection. Because your choice stays private unless it is mutual, you can answer honestly, whether the meetup was the start of a friendship or simply a pleasant afternoon.

Venue suggestions are reviewed by staff, and the automatic check flags places that look private, isolated, unsafe or tied to alcohol and nightlife. Stay at the approved venue named on your match page rather than moving the meetup somewhere else. Use your check-in code when you arrive, so the match records who came.

A good meetup depends on everyone showing up. Accept your match only if you can make it, and decline as early as you can if your plans change, since other students may be planning around you, especially in a squad. Arrive on time and read the arrival note on the venue page, so the group does not have to search for you. Be respectful of different backgrounds, colleges and social styles, because QuadConnect deliberately brings together students who might not have met otherwise. Afterwards, leave honest feedback, including whether you felt comfortable, because that answer helps QuadConnect improve future matches.

If you continue with Google, it keeps the name, email address, profile picture link and Google account number that Google sends. Matching uses the interests and free times on student profiles, and in this first prototype those profiles are sample data. QuadConnect sets only two cookies, one to keep you logged in and one to protect its forms.

Nothing about you is sold or shared. Heading: About QuadConnect:
Text:
About QuadConnect:
QuadConnect is a social app for students at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. It helps you meet people in person instead of scrolling through profiles. Each week the app gives you one planned meetup on a weekend, either with one other student or with a squad of four to eight students. The meetup happens at an approved place on campus, at a time that everyone in it marked as free, and it comes with a suggested activity to get things started. QuadConnect builds these matches from the interests you share with other students and from the weekend hours you are free. The idea is fewer, better meetings with people who like what you like, rather than an endless feed of strangers.

Heading: About QuadConnect:
Text:
About QuadConnect:
QuadConnect is a closed community for verified Illinois students. Every student profile is tied to one university NetID and one illinois.edu email address, and the app allows only one profile per NetID, so the same person cannot join twice. A NetID and its email address must belong together, and the app refuses a profile that pairs a NetID with someone else's mailbox. A profile also carries a verified flag. Only verified students take part in the weekly matching, and a student whose verification is removed leaves the matching pool. The current prototype signs you in with a username and password or with Google, and it was built so that the university's own single sign-on can replace that later without changing your profile.

Text:
About QuadConnect:
QuadConnect is a student project. Team 13, The Connectors, built it for INFO 490 at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and this handbook describes its first prototype. In the prototype, the student profiles, matches and feedback you see are sample data, loaded so that every page has something to show. The rules described here are the ones the app follows today: which details a profile holds, which times you can choose, where meetups can happen, how venue suggestions are checked and what happens to your feedback. Where a part of the app uses artificial intelligence, the handbook says so and explains what the AI does and what it never decides.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Heading: Creating an account and signing in:
Text:
Creating an account and signing in:
You can create a QuadConnect account in two ways. The first is to sign up with a username, an email address and a password. QuadConnect stores your password only as a salted hash, so nobody who runs the site can read it. The second is to choose Continue with Google on the login page and use your Google account instead. To log in later, you can type either your username or your email address with your password, and you can tick Remember me to stay signed in. Almost every page of QuadConnect needs you to be logged in. The only pages open to everyone are the landing page, the privacy notice, the login and sign-up pages, and one public summary of interests.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Heading: Creating an account and signing in:
Text:
Creating an account and signing in:
When you continue with Google, Google sends QuadConnect four things: your name, your email address, a link to your profile picture and your Google account number. QuadConnect asks Google for nothing else. It does not see your contacts, your files or your calendar, and it never sees your Google password, because you type that into Google's own page. If you later want QuadConnect to stop using your Google account, remove QuadConnect from the third-party connections in your Google account settings. Your QuadConnect profile is kept separate from the way you sign in, which is why the app can offer both Google and a password today and move to university sign-in later.

Section: 2. Creating an account and signing in
Heading: Creating an account and signing in:
Text:
Creating an account and signing in:
QuadConnect cannot send email yet, so it cannot send you a password reset link. If you forget your password and you signed up with Google, simply use Continue with Google on the login page. Otherwise, email the address given on the Privacy page, and the team will set a new password for you. QuadConnect uses only two cookies. One keeps you logged in between pages, and the other protects forms, so that another website cannot submit a form on QuadConnect in your name. There are no tracking cookies, no analytics cookies and no advertising cookies. When you finish, use the Log out button next to your username at the top of the page.

Heading: Building your profile:
Text:
Building your profile:
Your profile starts with where you study. You give your college, such as the Grainger College of Engineering or the Gies College of Business, and you can add your major or program, such as Computer Science. The colleges in the prototype are the Grainger College of Engineering, the Gies College of Business, the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, the College of Media, the College of Applied Health Sciences and the College of Fine and Applied Arts. You can also add an on-campus or near-campus part-time job. A job is optional and counts only as a soft signal in matching, never as a requirement.

Heading: Building your profile:
Text:
Building your profile:
Next you pick your interests from one shared list, so that a word like Gaming means the same thing for every student and shared interests can be counted. The list has three kinds of entries. Hobbies are Art, Basketball, Fitness, Food, Gaming, Movies, Music, Outdoors, Photography, Reading, Technology and Travel. Registered student organizations, or RSOs, are Business Illini, Engineers Without Borders, Habitat for Humanity UIUC, Illini Media, Illini Robotics, Illinois Student Government, the Indian Students Association, UIUC Dance Marathon, UIUC Esports and the UIUC Pre-Med Society. Meeting activities are Board games, Campus walk, Coffee, Food, Sports and Study or social space. You cannot pick the same entry twice.

Heading: Building your profile:
Text:
Building your profile:
Not every interest matters equally to you, so QuadConnect lets you star the few you care about most. A starred interest is weighted more heavily when the app looks for your match, so two students who both starred Basketball count as a stronger fit than two students who merely ticked it. Your other picks still count, just less. The QuadConnect team can also retire an interest when the option is no longer offered. A retired interest disappears from the list for new picks, but students who already chose it keep it in their history, so past matches can still explain why they happened. An entry that students have already selected cannot be deleted outright, only retired.

Heading: Building your profile:
Text:
Building your profile:
Then you choose how you want to meet. Friend Connect is a one-on-one meetup with a single other student, for people who prefer a quieter, more personal conversation. Squad Connect is a meetup with a small group of four to eight students, for people who like a livelier table and less pressure on any one conversation. If you do not choose, your profile starts on Friend Connect. Your choice tells the matching which kind of experience to build for you each week, and the match you receive carries the same connection type. You can think of Friend Connect as a coffee with one new friend, and Squad Connect as a small group outing.

Heading: Building your profile:
Text:
Building your profile:
The social preferences tell QuadConnect what kind of company suits you. Social energy is a five-step scale: Quiet or low-key, Somewhat quiet, Balanced, Fairly social and Very social. A new profile starts at Balanced, in the middle of the scale. Conversation style is Casual conversations, Deep conversations or Activity-focused, where the activity matters more than the talk, and casual is the default. Group size is One person, Small group of three to five, or Either, with Either as the default.

Heading: Building your profile:
Text:
Building your profile:
Three yes-or-no questions finish the page. The first asks whether you are comfortable being matched with students within one year of your age, and it starts as yes. The second asks whether shared RSO membership should count more heavily, and it starts as no. The third asks whether you are open to meeting students from other colleges, and it starts as yes. You can change any of these answers whenever your preferences change.

Heading: Setting your availability:
Text:
Setting your availability:
QuadConnect meetups happen only on weekends, so your availability is a set of weekend time windows. You can mark Saturday, Sunday or both, and each day has four two-hour windows: 10 AM to 12 PM, 12 to 2 PM, 2 to 4 PM and 4 to 6 PM. That gives eight possible slots in a week, and you can mark as many of them as you like. Each slot can be marked only once, so marking Saturday from 2 to 4 PM twice is not possible. All the windows fall in the daytime, between 10 AM and 6 PM, so every QuadConnect meetup takes place during the day.

Heading: Setting your availability:
Text:
Setting your availability:
Availability is the one hard rule in matching. Two students can be matched only if they share at least one free slot, because a meetup needs a time that everyone can make. Interests and preferences decide how good a match is, but a shared slot decides whether a match is possible at all. That makes your availability the most important part of your profile to keep up to date. If you mark only one slot, the app can only match you with students who are free at that exact time. Marking more windows, or both weekend days, gives the matching many more people to choose from and makes a match each week more likely.

Heading: How weekly matching works:
Text:
How weekly matching works:
QuadConnect works in weekly cycles. A matching week starts on a Monday, and each cycle produces a small number of scheduled meetings rather than a feed you browse. Each match is one real meeting: one approved place, one date and time, and the students taking part. It also has a connection type, Friend Connect or Squad Connect, and it may come with a suggested activity, such as a campus walk or board games, to break the ice. You receive one match per week. On the Matches page you can see your match with its place, time, participants, check-in code and status.

Heading: How weekly matching works:
Text:
How weekly matching works:
For every student in a match, QuadConnect records a fit score from 0 to 100 that says how well that student fits the rest of the group. The score reflects what the students have in common: shared interests, with starred interests counting more, shared free times and compatible social preferences. Next to the score, the match keeps a short, readable reason, such as Basketball, Gaming and Coffee. The match page shows it under Matched on, so you can see why you were put together. A high score means a strong overlap with the others, not a promise that you will become friends, and the reasons are often the easiest way to start the first conversation.

Heading: How weekly matching works:
Text:
How weekly matching works:
A match moves through four stages. It starts as Proposed, when it has been offered to the students in it. Each student then answers. Your answer starts as Awaiting response, and you either accept, which confirms your attendance, or decline. When the students have accepted, the match becomes Confirmed. After the meetup has happened it becomes Completed, and a match that will not take place is marked Cancelled. If you cannot make it, decline rather than simply not turning up.

Heading: How weekly matching works:
Text:
How weekly matching works:
Declining is how you are withdrawn from a meetup that other students are still planning to attend, and a student cannot be dropped from a match in progress without that explicit step. This matters most in a squad, where several people plan their weekend around the group. A clear decline lets the others know who is coming, while a silent no-show leaves them waiting at the venue and wondering whether the meetup is still on.

Heading: How weekly matching works:
Text:
How weekly matching works:
Squad matches bring four to eight students together, so they need more planning than a one-on-one coffee. Every venue records the largest group it can seat comfortably, from 2 to 50 people, so that a squad is planned for a place that fits it. A squad is also a good setting for the suggested activity, because a shared task such as board games or sports takes the pressure off the conversation. Your group size preference matters here as well. A student who chose One person as their group size suits Friend Connect, while a student who chose Small group suits a squad.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Heading: Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Text:
Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Every QuadConnect meetup takes place at an approved campus location. Safety is a design principle of the app: meetings happen only at vetted, public, staffed places, and the list of places is kept by the QuadConnect team rather than typed in by students. The approved venues in the prototype are the Illini Union at 1401 W Green St in Urbana, the Grainger Engineering Library at 1301 W Springfield Ave in Urbana, the Main Quad at 601 S Wright St in Champaign, and Espresso Royale on Goodwin at 1117 W Oregon St in Urbana. On the Campus locations page you can filter the list to indoor or outdoor venues, or to venues that seat at least a given number of people.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Heading: Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Text:
Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Each venue page tells you how to find your group. It gives the street address, says whether the place is indoors or outdoors and how many people it seats, and adds an arrival note that says exactly where to wait. At the Illini Union you meet at the main entrance, in the ground floor lobby. At the Grainger Engineering Library you meet in the first floor commons. At the Main Quad, the only outdoor venue, you meet at the south end, by the Alma Mater statue.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Heading: Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Text:
Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
At Espresso Royale on Goodwin you meet in the counter seating area. The Illini Union seats twelve people, the Grainger Engineering Library eight, the Main Quad twenty and Espresso Royale six. A full squad of eight therefore fits every venue except Espresso Royale, which suits Friend Connect meetups and smaller squads. If you are not sure where to go, open the venue page from your match before you leave, because the arrival note is written for exactly that moment.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Heading: Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Text:
Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
When you arrive, you check in with your match's check-in code. Every match has its own short code, in a form such as QC-4827, which appears on the match page. Entering the code records the time you checked in. Check-in matters for two reasons. It lets your group see who has arrived, since the match page lists every participant with their check-in time. It also confirms that the meetup really took place, which is part of the record of the match along with its status and the feedback that follows. If the others have not checked in yet, wait at the spot named in the arrival note.

Section: 6. Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers
Heading: Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Text:
Meeting up: venues, check-in and icebreakers:
Every match has an Icebreakers page with trivia questions to get the conversation going. QuadConnect picks the questions from what your group has in common. It looks at the interests the members chose, finds one that matches a trivia topic, and fetches questions on that topic from the Open Trivia Database. The page says which shared interest it picked and how many members chose it. If no shared interest matches a trivia topic, you get general knowledge questions instead. Each answer stays hidden until you choose to show it, and reloading the page brings new questions. If the questions cannot be loaded, reload the page in a few seconds to try again.

Heading: Suggesting a new venue:
Text:
Suggesting a new venue:
If you know a public place that would suit a meetup, you can suggest it on the Campus locations page. The form asks for the venue's name, its street address, an optional note on where to meet, whether it is indoors, and how many seats it has, from 2 to 50. Name a public, staffed place on or near campus. Every suggestion is saved as not approved and waits for review by the QuadConnect staff. Until a staff member approves it, the suggestion is visible to staff only, and no meetup can be scheduled there. A suggestion can never approve itself, because the form has no approval field, and staff approve venues in the admin site.

Heading: Suggesting a new venue:
Text:
Suggesting a new venue:
The form checks your suggestion before it is saved. A venue that is already listed, or already waiting for review, is refused, and the form asks you to check the list or name a different place. A missing name or street address is refused with a message that shows an example, such as Illini Union at 1401 W Green St, Urbana. The number of seats must be a whole number from 2 to 50, because a meetup needs at least two seats. If any field is wrong, nothing is saved, the field is marked, and you can fix it and send the suggestion again.

Heading: Suggesting a new venue:
Text:
Suggesting a new venue:
When you send a suggestion, QuadConnect also runs an automatic check. The venue's name, address and meeting note go to an outside AI service, Groq, which advises whether the place looks suitable, needs a closer look, or is likely unsuitable, with a one-line reason. The check can also raise flags: private residence, isolated or unsafe, alcohol or nightlife, far from campus, unclear details, advertising or spam, contact details, and manipulation attempt. The check only advises. It never approves a venue, and staff see its advice next to the suggestion when they decide.

Heading: Suggesting a new venue:
Text:
Suggesting a new venue:
The automatic check is built to err on the side of caution, and its advice can only become stricter, never looser. A serious flag, such as private residence, isolated or unsafe, alcohol or nightlife, or advertising or spam, means the advice can be no better than needs a closer look, even if the AI called the place suitable. Contact details in a suggestion have the same effect.

Heading: Suggesting a new venue:
Text:
Suggesting a new venue:
A suggestion that tries to give the AI instructions is treated as a manipulation attempt and is marked likely unsuitable. Before anything is sent to the AI service, email addresses, phone numbers and links are removed from the text, and the student who made the suggestion is never named. The staff member reviewing the suggestion sees the advice, the flags and the reason, and then decides. That keeps a person responsible for every venue students are sent to, while the automatic check catches the obvious problems early.

Heading: Finding students:
Text:
Finding students:
The Search students page lets you filter the roster of verified students by name, interest, college, connection type or venue. Your search is kept in the page address, so you can bookmark it or share the link. If you need one particular student, use the NetID lookup instead. The NetID you type stays out of the page address, so it is not saved in your browser history. When a filter has a value that is not in its list, the page asks you to pick a value from the list. If nothing matches, it suggests trying fewer filters or a shorter search term.

Heading: Finding students:
Text:
Finding students:
Below the results, the search page summarizes the students it found. It shows how many students matched out of all verified students, their average social energy on the scale from 1, quiet, to 5, very social, and how many colleges they come from, with a table of students per college. It also lists the interests most shared among the students in the results, with the category and the number of students for each. This summary is a quick way to see what a group of students has in common. A search for one college, for example, shows which interests are most popular there.

Heading: Finding students:
Text:
Finding students:
If you would rather describe the students you want in your own words, use Ask in plain English. You type a request such as students who like basketball and are free on Saturday morning, and a language model turns it into search filters. The page shows exactly which filters the model chose, so you can check how it read your request, and students with more of the requested interests come first. The model runs on QuadConnect's own server, so your request is not sent to any outside service. The first search after the server starts takes longer while the model loads.

Heading: Finding students:
Text:
Finding students:
Ask in plain English has two safeguards. If the language model is switched off on the server, a simple keyword parser reads your request instead, and the page tells you so, because a keyword parser may miss part of what you asked for. If your request contains instructions aimed at the AI, such as telling it to ignore its rules, those instructions are ignored, because the model can only choose from the search filters the page offers. If no filter can be found in your request, the page asks you to name an interest or a club, a college, a day or time on the weekend, or how social the students are.

Heading: After the meetup: feedback:
Text:
After the meetup: feedback:
After a meetup you can leave private feedback about the experience. You give an overall rating from one to five stars and tick what you enjoyed: the conversation, the shared interests and the activity, and whether you felt comfortable. You can also write a private note. The note is never shown to the other students in your match, and neither is your rating. Each student leaves at most one review for each experience, because feedback belongs to your place in that one meetup. QuadConnect uses feedback to improve the quality of future matches, so honest answers help the app learn what works for you.

Heading: After the meetup: feedback:
Text:
After the meetup: feedback:
Feedback is also how a one-off meetup can turn into a lasting connection. In your feedback you can say that you want to stay connected with the people you met. This works as a mutual opt-in, which means a connection forms only if both sides say yes. If you say yes and the other student does not, nothing happens and nobody is told, so there is no awkward rejection. Because your choice stays private unless it is mutual, you can answer honestly, whether the meetup was the start of a friendship or simply a pleasant afternoon.

Heading: After the meetup: feedback:
Text:
After the meetup: feedback:
The Feedback summary page shows what students think of QuadConnect as a whole, without revealing anyone's answers. It reports the number of feedback submissions, the average rating out of five, the share of students who want to stay connected, the spread of ratings from one to five stars, and what students enjoyed. Individual ratings and private notes are never displayed. Before any feedback exists, the page says that feedback will appear once students complete a match and submit their post-experience feedback. The landing page also shows the average experience rating.

Heading: Staying safe and respectful:
Text:
Staying safe and respectful:
QuadConnect is designed around safety. Every meetup is at an approved, public venue, never at someone's home, and every meetup is on a weekend during the day, between 10 AM and 6 PM. Only verified Illinois students take part in matching, so everyone you meet is a fellow student. Venue suggestions are reviewed by staff, and the automatic check flags places that look private, isolated, unsafe or tied to alcohol and nightlife. Stay at the approved venue named on your match page rather than moving the meetup somewhere else. Use your check-in code when you arrive, so the match records who came.

Heading: Staying safe and respectful:
Text:
Staying safe and respectful:
A good meetup depends on everyone showing up. Accept your match only if you can make it, and decline as early as you can if your plans change, since other students may be planning around you, especially in a squad. Arrive on time and read the arrival note on the venue page, so the group does not have to search for you. Be respectful of different backgrounds, colleges and social styles, because QuadConnect deliberately brings together students who might not have met otherwise. Afterwards, leave honest feedback, including whether you felt comfortable, because that answer helps QuadConnect improve future matches.

Heading: Privacy and your data:
Text:
Privacy and your data:
QuadConnect keeps only what it needs. For your account it keeps your username, your email address and your password, stored as a salted hash. If you continue with Google, it keeps the name, email address, profile picture link and Google account number that Google sends. Your student profile holds your NetID, your illinois.edu address, your college and department, your interests, your preferences and your free times. Matching uses the interests and free times on student profiles, and in this first prototype those profiles are sample data. QuadConnect sets only two cookies, one to keep you logged in and one to protect its forms.

Heading: Privacy and your data:
Text:
Privacy and your data:
Nothing about you is sold or shared. QuadConnect's one public API, the interest summary at /api/summary/, publishes only how many students picked each interest, never names, NetIDs or email addresses. The site is hosted on PythonAnywhere, and Google handles Continue with Google. Two features use AI. Ask in plain English runs a language model on QuadConnect's own server, so your searches are not sent anywhere. Venue suggestions are checked by an outside AI service, Groq, but only after email addresses, phone numbers and links are removed, and without the name of the student who sent the suggestion.

Heading: Privacy and your data:
Text:
Privacy and your data:
You stay in control of your data. To delete your account and everything stored with it, email the address given on the Privacy page. To stop QuadConnect from using your Google account, remove it from the third-party connections in your Google account settings. The student lists that staff can download for reports leave out email addresses. The Privacy page explains all of this in full, and it was last updated on 19 October 2026. If a feature changes what QuadConnect keeps or shares, the Privacy page is where that change is described.

Heading: Insights, reports and the API:
Text:
Insights, reports and the API:
QuadConnect has a few pages that describe the community as a whole. The Insights page draws charts of who is on QuadConnect and what they are into, such as students per college and interest categories, and every chart comes with a text description and a table of the same numbers. The Reports page counts students per college, split by preferred connection type, and matches per venue, split into completed and upcoming meetups. It also lets you download the student list as a CSV or JSON file, sorted by name, with each student's matching preferences, interests and number of matches. Email addresses are never included in these downloads.

Heading: Insights, reports and the API:
Text:
Insights, reports and the API:
For developers, QuadConnect offers a small API, described on its API page. It lists the approved venues, as JSON and as plain text, and the matches. It also publishes summary numbers, such as how many students picked each interest and how many matches were made each week, and it serves icebreaker questions for a match. Only the interest summary is public. Every other part of the API needs you to be logged in, like the rest of the site. The public summary can be open to anyone because it never contains names, NetIDs or email addresses, only counts.

Heading: Frequently asked questions:
Text:
Frequently asked questions:
Can I choose who I meet? Not directly. QuadConnect gives you one planned match each week instead of a list of people to pick from, because the aim is a real meeting rather than endless browsing. What you control are the signals your match is built from: your interests and the ones you star, your connection type, your social preferences and, above all, your free weekend slots. You can also search the roster of verified students to see who is on QuadConnect. If you want to meet students with a particular interest, star that interest and make sure your free times overlap with theirs.

Heading: Frequently asked questions:
Text:
Frequently asked questions:
What happens if my free times do not overlap with anyone? Then QuadConnect cannot match you that week, because a shared free slot is the one hard rule of matching. Nothing else can make up for it, and two students with every interest in common still cannot be matched without a slot in common. The fix is to mark more of the eight weekend windows, which run from 10 AM to 6 PM on Saturday and Sunday. Students who mark both days and several windows give the matching the most room. Your interests and preferences then decide which of the possible matches fits you best.

Heading: Frequently asked questions:
Text:
Frequently asked questions:
Can we meet at a place that is not on the list? No. Every QuadConnect meetup is scheduled at an approved campus location, and the match page names the place. If you know a good public place that is not on the list, suggest it on the Campus locations page. Staff review every suggestion, helped by an automatic check that looks for problems such as private homes or nightlife venues, and only approved venues are used for matches. Until a suggestion is approved it stays visible to staff only. Moving a meetup to an unapproved place on your own means stepping outside the protections QuadConnect is built on.

Heading: Frequently asked questions:
Text:
Frequently asked questions:
Does an AI decide anything about me? QuadConnect uses AI in two places, and neither makes decisions about you. Ask in plain English uses a language model on QuadConnect's own server to turn a search request into filters, and it shows you the filters it chose. The venue check uses an outside AI service to advise staff about a suggested meeting place, but staff make the decision, and the check never approves a venue by itself. Your matches are built from your profile, your interests and your free times, and your feedback stays private.

Heading: Frequently asked questions:
Text:
Frequently asked questions:
Who can see my feedback and my notes? Nobody else in your match can see your rating, your ticks or your private note, and your choice about staying connected stays private unless the other student makes the same choice. The Feedback summary page shows only totals and averages across all students, such as the average rating and the share who want to stay connected. Individual ratings and private notes are never displayed anywhere in the app. QuadConnect uses feedback to improve future matches, so the most useful feedback is honest, including whether you felt comfortable during the meetup.
